To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the depth of absorption lines is determined primarily by cloud properties and that the relative strengths of molecular bands provide diagnostics for the atmospheric composition, temperature, and temperature structure, although these diagnostics are not completely independent.

the spectrum ratio (λ) is a useful tool for studying the atmospheres of transiting EGPs, and the diagnostic power of (λ) is limited by the effects of clouds, the need for high spectral resolution and high S/N, and the degeneracies among the various atmospheric parameters.

the transmission spectrum ratio (λ) is a powerful diagnostic of extrasolar giant planet (EGP) atmospheres; that (λ) is determined primarily by the height of the first atmospheric layer to become opaque to tangential stellar radiation; and that this height depends on the atmospheric scale height, the opacity ratio between strong lines and the continuum, and the cloud properties.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (1) What are the most useful diagnostics for the physical conditions and composition of EGP atmospheres? (2) How can we extract the maximum amount of useful information from a given set of observations? and (3) What are the requirements for future observations?
the development of methods for extracting information from transmission spectra of transiting EGPs.
the development of methods to extract physical information about extrasolar planets from the spectra of their host stars.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, although the prospects for the detection of absorption features in the spectrum of HD 209458 are good, the interpretation will be difficult.
the atmospheres of EGps are not yet understood well enough to permit confident use of their spectra as diagnostics of their physical properties.
the diagnostic potential of the transmission spectrum for EGPs is great, but the observational challenges are daunting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the atmospheres of close-in EGPs are likely to be cloudy and have a heavy-element content of at least 0.1 times solar, with a range of possible temperatures.
we have developed the tools to interpret the spectra of extrasolar giant planets.
we have shown that the transmission spectra of extrasolar giant planets contain a great deal of information, but that the observational challenges are formidable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the atmospheres of close-in EGPs are sufficiently complex that the interpretation of transit spectra will be difficult.
, although the spectra of EGPs will be difficult to observe and interpret, they will provide unique and powerful diagnostics of the atmospheres of these planets.
